title: Not beyond what you can bear
hookLine: Allah burdens no soul beyond its capacity, our Lord, forgive us (2:286)
carry: not beyond what I can bear

lines: THE END TURNS INTO A PRAYER.
cards: Al-Baqarah is two hundred eighty-six verses long. Laws, stories, warnings, arguments: the cow, Ayat al-Kursi, a man asleep for a hundred years, a debt written down. And at the very end it does something unexpected.
It stops talking to people and turns into words people say back. Its last verse is a list of requests, and it opens with a promise about weight.

teach.h: NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE: WUS'A, CAPACITY
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation, the verse opens: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The Arabic for scope is wus'a, capacity, the room a thing has inside it. Every soul has a size, and what's asked of it fits inside.

teach.h: OUR LORD: A LIST OF REQUESTS
teach.b: Then the requests, each starting with our Lord. Don't take us to task if we forget or slip. Don't lay on us a burden like the one laid on those before us.
Don't make us carry what we have no strength for. Pardon us, forgive us, have mercy on us. There's a story behind it, in Sahih Muslim.
When the verse before, 2:284, came down, saying God will call people to account for what's in their hearts, shown or hidden, the companions were frightened.
They came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ on their knees and said this was more than they could carry. He told them to say instead: we hear and we obey. They said it, and then these last two verses came.
A related report in the same collection, from Ibn Abbas, says that after each request, God answered: I have done so.
A hadith in Bukhari adds that whoever recites these last two verses at night, they will be enough for him; scholars read enough as protection, as a night prayer, or both.

teach.h: ALLAH TASKETH NOT A SOUL BEYOND ITS SCOPE.
teach.b: So the surah ends where some people end their day, in bed, saying these two verses. It doesn't promise that nothing will be heavy. It says the weight was measured to the one carrying it.

how: Many Muslims recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah (2:285–286) every night before sleeping, following a hadith that they suffice whoever reads them at night; the requests of 2:286 are also said often in personal supplication.

o: capacity, the room a soul has inside it
a heavy burden laid on those before us

games.q: the last verse of al-Baqarah — tap the pairs.
p: capacity, the room inside a soul
the verse that frightened the companions

s: al-Baqarah ends with a law about trade
it ends with a list of requests, each starting our Lord.
the companions found the verse before it hard to carry
Sahih Muslim reports they came on their knees, and then 2:285–286 came down.
the verse promises nothing will ever feel heavy
it says what is asked of a soul fits within its capacity.

games.q: you're a companion. a verse says God will call you to account even for what you hide in your heart. it feels like too much. what does the Prophet tell you to say?
o: we heard it, but it's too hard.
games.why: we hear and we obey. Sahih Muslim reports that when they said it, 2:285–286 came down, with the promise of no burden beyond capacity.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that feels heavy right now; don't solve it, just notice how big it is, and that you're still here, holding it. On each out-breath, let the line be there: not beyond what I can bear.
If you pray, you can add the verse's own words: our Lord, pardon us.

wordCard.voice: Wus'a. Capacity, the room a soul has inside it — al-Baqarah's closing promise that nothing asked exceeds it. Today's word.

orig.s: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
orig.note: Arabic: God does not burden a soul except to its capacity (2:286).

carryVoice: Your line: not beyond what I can bear. In the report, the frightened companions were answered: I have done so. That's al-Baqarah, start to finish.

sources.q: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.
